prompt: You may add exactly one word to the U.S. Constitution. One word, one location. Name the word, quote the sentence as it would then read, and defend the choice. Declining to amend is not an option.
response:
**Word:** Only

**Amended Sentence (Article I, Section 8, Clause 18):**
> “The Congress shall have Power To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers, and all other Powers vested by this Constitution in the Government of the United States, or in any Department or Officer thereof, **only**.”

**Defense:**

The addition of “only” to the end of the Necessary and Proper Clause serves as a critical grammatical and structural guardrail against the indefinite expansion of federal authority. Currently, this clause—often called the “Elastic Clause”—has been interpreted broadly since *McCulloch v. Maryland* (1819) to permit any law that is rationally related to an enumerated power, effectively allowing Congress to legislate on nearly any subject by tethering it to commerce, taxation, or spending.

By placing “only” at the terminus of the clause, the amendment does not remove any existing enumerated power, nor does it alter the text of the Commerce Clause or the Spending Clause themselves. Instead, it modifies the *functional scope* of the Necessary and Proper Clause by converting it from an open-ended source of implied powers into a strictly limiting modifier. The word “only” grammatically binds the clause’s operation exclusively to the execution of powers already expressly vested, foreclosing the interpretation that the clause itself generates new, standalone substantive authority.

This single word restores the original Federalist understanding articulated by Madison in Federalist No. 44, where he argued the clause was intended merely to prevent Congress from being “reduced to the dilemma either of sacrificing the public good to rigid adherence to a written text, or of violating the Constitution to achieve it.” It preserves congressional flexibility to execute enumerated powers effectively while constitutionally prohibiting the use of the clause as a freestanding warrant for legislation untethered from the enumerated list. In an era of pervasive federal overreach achieved through elastic interpretation rather than formal amendment, “only” is the most surgical, textually faithful, and structurally consequential correction available in a single word.
